newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Stable prices, dinar priority of Yugo econ policy.
newsitem.headline: Stable prices, dinar priority of Yugo econ policy.

text.p: The Yugoslav government is committed to its 1996 policy of creating an open, export-oriented economy and preserving price and dinar stability, the Belgrade daily Vecernje Novosti reported on Tuesday.

"The federal government's priority is to preserve the stability of prices and the dinar through measures and mechanisms founded on market principles," the pro-government newspaper quoted Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Jovan Zebic as saying.

According to Vecernje Novosti, the government aimed for 12.5 percent GDP growth for 1996, with industrial output to expand by 10.5 percent, agriculture by three percent, and other sectors by 20.8 percent.
Industrial output in the first seven months rose 3.8 percent compared with the same period last year and independent analysts said the targeted figures were unrealistic.

"It is hard to estimate GDP growth. We do not know how it is calculated and if all losses will be included in the figure," Stojan Stamenkovic, a prominent economist at the Belgrade Institute of Economic Sciences, told Reuters.

"As for industrial output, if monetary support for it increases, it will be higher than last year, but at most by 6.5 percent," Stamenkovic said, but added such growth could not be sustained for long without fresh capital.

Speaking in the western Serbian town of Sabac on Monday, Zebic said a budget balance was being maintained and that banks' liquidity had improved in July and August, but export results were still below expectations.
"Despite the 7.2 percent increase compared to last year, export results are still unfavourable" Zebic said.
The trade deficit for January-July reached nearly $1 billion, with exports worth $0.94 and imports $1.937 billion.

To overcome the crippling effects of three years of international sanctions and the break-up of the integral Yugoslav market, Zebic highlighted a number of new laws aimed at smoothing Yugoslavia's return to the world economy.

"The foreign investments and ownership transformation laws in particular are aimed at greater liberalisation, adjustment to conditions after the suspension of sanctions, and speedier reintegration of our economy in world economic trends." -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
